learning_objective: 🎯 Look up! Discover the invisible blanket of gases, water, and dust that keeps Earth from freezing, protects us from solar radiation, and gives us weather.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: The air is a mix of gases. Nitrogen makes up 78%, and Oxygen makes up 21%. The remaining 1% includes Argon, Carbon Dioxide, and other trace gases. The atmosphere also holds vital water vapour and tiny dust particles.
This is the lowest layer where we live. Almost all weather (clouds, rain, storms) happens here. As you go higher in the troposphere, the temperature drops. This is why mountains are cold!
Above the troposphere is the stratosphere. Commercial airplanes fly here to avoid storms. It contains the crucial Ozone Layer, which absorbs harmful Ultraviolet (UV) rays from the sun.

Above the stratosphere are the Mesosphere (where meteors burn up), the Thermosphere (where temperatures skyrocket and radio waves bounce back to Earth), and finally the Exosphere, which fades into space.

fun_activity.title: ☁️ The Dust Particle Sunbeam
fun_activity.instructions: Darken a room completely during the day and leave just a small crack in the curtains for a single beam of sunlight to enter. Look closely at the beam. The floating 'sparkles' you see are dust particles, which are crucial for forming clouds in our atmosphere!

exam_tips: 📌 Know the exact percentages: Nitrogen 78.08% and Oxygen 20.95%. Carbon Dioxide is only 0.036% but plays a massive role in the greenhouse effect.
📌 The 'Tropopause' is the boundary separating the Troposphere and Stratosphere.
📌 The Ionosphere (located in the Thermosphere) is responsible for reflecting radio waves back to Earth, making wireless communication possible.
quick_recap: ⭐ The atmosphere is composed of gases, water vapour, and dust particles.
⭐ Water vapour and dust particles are heavily concentrated only in the lower atmosphere.
⭐ The atmosphere is divided into five distinct layers based on temperature variations.
